interview_metadata.name: Kailea Rubel
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born over in Pascagoula and raised mostly in Moss Point, in a big white Southern Baptist family where somebody was always cooking, singing, fixing a roof, or checking on a neighbor. My grandparents lived close by, and I grew up with church suppers, hurricane boards stacked in the shed, and Friday night football being a real event. School was not easy for me. I got through the eleventh grade, but after my mama got sick for a spell and money was tight, I left before graduating and went to helping at home, babysitting, cleaning, and doing whatever little jobs came along. I married Tommy Rubel when I was in my twenties. We raised two children, Marissa and Caleb, and I put a lot of myself into church, school fundraisers, potlucks, and neighborhood events. Hurricanes shaped me too, especially Katrina, because you learn real quick who checks on who and who knows where the batteries and water are. These days I am not in the paid workforce, but I coordinate volunteers at church and local events, bake when people need pies or biscuits, garden, quilt, sing in choir, and I am studying toward my GED because I still want that done.

follow_ups.question: When you picture your childhood home, what details come back first?
follow_ups.response: The smell of biscuits, my daddy's work boots by the door, and my mama keeping a calendar with everybody's church meetings and doctor appointments. We had relatives drifting in and out all the time, so quiet was rare.

follow_ups.question: What made leaving school happen when it did?
follow_ups.response: It was not one dramatic day. Mama needed help, I was already behind, and I felt more useful earning a little and keeping the house moving than sitting in class embarrassed.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was after Katrina. Our place was damaged but standing, and for a while Tommy and I talked about leaving the coast altogether, maybe going closer to his cousin in Alabama. I was tired, scared, and mad at how long everything took. But our church started organizing meals, supply lists, and rides for older folks, and I found I was good at getting names on a clipboard and matching people to jobs. I chose to stay and help rebuild our little routines instead of starting over somewhere else. That decision turned me into the person people call when they need an event pulled together or a family checked on.

follow_ups.question: What was the first organizing job you remember doing after the storm?
follow_ups.response: I made a list of who needed tarps, insulin kept cold, or a ride to get paperwork done. It was notebook paper, a church phone tree, and a lot of porch visits.

follow_ups.question: Did Tommy agree with staying?
follow_ups.response: He was worried about work and money, but he knew my heart was here. Once his job settled back down, he was on board.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was both. The storm pushed us, but staying was a conscious choice after a lot of kitchen-table talks and prayer.

follow_ups.question: Do you remember a specific moment when the decision felt settled?
follow_ups.response: Yes, when I was packing canned goods at church and realized I did not want to be needed somewhere else; I wanted to be useful right here.

follow_ups.question: Who did you talk to about it?
follow_ups.response: Tommy, my mama, and our pastor's wife. They all told me not to make a fear decision.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. FEMA and insurance were hard to navigate, and I wish there had been clearer local help for paperwork and repairs. The church helped more personally than any agency did.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Somebody sitting down with families and explaining forms, deadlines, and contractor warnings in plain language.

follow_ups.question: Did that experience affect how you volunteer now?
follow_ups.response: Absolutely. I try to make sign-up sheets and instructions simple because people in crisis cannot chase details.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Tommy Rubel. He works maintenance around the shipyard side of things, and he is quieter than me but steady. We have two grown children. Marissa is 27, married, and lives in Ocean Springs with my little grandson Eli, who is four. Caleb is 22 and still finding his footing; he works warehouse shifts and comes by most Sundays. My mama, Darlene, is still in Jackson County, and I check on her a few times a week. Family for me is not just holidays. It is who gets a casserole when they are sick, who needs a ride, who is coming for Sunday lunch, and who calls when the weather turns bad.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your children?
follow_ups.response: Marissa and Eli usually come over twice a month, more if Tommy grills. Caleb is more like every week, sometimes just to raid leftovers.

follow_ups.question: What is your relationship with Tommy like day to day?
follow_ups.response: We have our routines. He handles a lot of repairs and yard equipment, and I handle the calendar, bills, cooking, and family communication.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have an older sister, Renee, in Gautier. We are close but can fuss over details because we are both bossy in our own way.

follow_ups.question: How often do you and Renee talk?
follow_ups.response: A few times a week by phone, and we see each other at church events or family meals.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually fuss about?
follow_ups.response: Food timing, money decisions for Mama, or which one of us promised what to which cousin.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friends are women from church and the walking club. Linda sings alto beside me in choir, and Miss Carol quilts with me on Wednesday afternoons. I also spend time with a few festival committee folks because once you have survived planning Mardi Gras barricades and food tents together, you know each other's nerves. We text about prayer requests, recipes, volunteer gaps, and sometimes just gossip about local happenings.

follow_ups.question: Who would you call first in a non-family emergency?
follow_ups.response: Linda, because she answers the phone and she knows how to stay calm.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually spend time with friends?
follow_ups.response: Church fellowship hall, the walking path after gardening club, or somebody's kitchen table.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Moss Point, not far from people who have known each other a long time. It is a mix of older homes, working families, retirees, churches, empty lots, and folks doing the best they can. You hear lawn mowers, dogs, church vans, and sometimes teenagers with music too loud. I like being close to the river and close enough to Pascagoula and the coast for errands. It is not fancy, but there is history here, and people still wave from porches.

follow_ups.question: What places do you go to most in the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: Church, the grocery, the library sometimes, and the community center when there is an event or meeting.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors know one another?
follow_ups.response: Some do very well. The newer renters keep more to themselves, but the long-time folks notice if your trash can is not out or your lights are off.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe in the daytime and cautious at night. We lock doors, keep porch lights on, and I do not leave packages sitting out.

follow_ups.question: Has something happened that made you cautious?
follow_ups.response: A few car break-ins on nearby streets and some drug activity people talk about.

follow_ups.question: Do you walk in the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but usually mornings or with the walking group, not late by myself.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is roots, family, church, and the water nearby. The downside is storm worry, limited jobs, and houses that need more repair than people can afford.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you from moving?
follow_ups.response: My family, my church, and knowing how to navigate this place.

follow_ups.question: What would you change if you could?
follow_ups.response: More youth programs, better drainage, and more reliable transportation for older folks.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me and Tommy in the house full time. Caleb stays over now and then if his shift runs late or he has laundry to do, but he does not live here. My grandson Eli spends the night maybe once or twice a month. It is a small household most days, though Sundays can make it feel full.

follow_ups.question: Who handles most household chores?
follow_ups.response: I do cooking, laundry, bills, and inside cleaning. Tommy handles mowing, repairs, and heavier lifting.

follow_ups.question: Do you have pets?
follow_ups.response: No pets right now. I like animals, but I do not want one more daily responsibility.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone permanent is just me and Tommy.

follow_ups.question: Does Caleb keep belongings there?
follow_ups.response: A few old boxes, but not enough to count as living here.

follow_ups.question: Any planned changes to the household?
follow_ups.response: No, not unless family needs temporary help.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Eli, my grandson, stays sometimes, and Caleb may spend a night.

follow_ups.question: How often does Eli stay?
follow_ups.response: Usually one weekend night every few weeks.

follow_ups.question: Where do guests sleep?
follow_ups.response: In the spare room with the quilt frame folded against the wall.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody who usually lives here is away.

follow_ups.question: Any family temporarily in care elsewhere?
follow_ups.response: No, thankfully.

follow_ups.question: Any students away from home?
follow_ups.response: No, my children are grown and local.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Mondays I usually clean, plan meals, and check the church calendar. Tuesdays and Thursdays I garden early if it is not too hot, then run errands or work on GED lessons in the afternoon. Wednesday is often quilting at church. Friday nights in season are high school football. Sundays are church, choir, and family food. I keep a paper planner because if I only put things in my phone, I miss details.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually get up?
follow_ups.response: Around 6:15, earlier in summer so I can water before the heat.

follow_ups.question: When do you study for the GED?
follow_ups.response: Mostly midafternoon, about three days a week, with math taking the most patience.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I am not working a regular paid job right now. I do unpaid volunteer coordination for church and community events, and sometimes I sell baked goods informally when someone asks for a pecan pie, biscuits, or cobbler. That is not steady income. Most of my work is scheduling volunteers, calling people, shopping for supplies, setting up tables, and keeping costs down.

follow_ups.question: How many hours do you volunteer in a busy week?
follow_ups.response: During Mardi Gras or a church dinner, it can be 20 hours easy. A normal week is more like 6 to 10.

follow_ups.question: Do you want paid work again?
follow_ups.response: Yes, part time if it fits. I would like community center work or something with children or health aide training.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help my mama with appointments and groceries, and I keep our emergency supplies checked during hurricane season. I also manage the household budget every Friday morning when Tommy's pay hits. Choir practice is Wednesday evening, and I try to walk with the club twice a week. Dental habits are my weak spot; I brush, but after sweets I forget flossing more than I should.

follow_ups.question: What is in your hurricane routine?
follow_ups.response: Water, batteries, canned goods, medications, important papers in a plastic folder, and knowing who in church needs help.

follow_ups.question: Who depends on you most each week?
follow_ups.response: Tommy for the home schedule, Mama for errands, and the church ladies for event details.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest change is studying for my GED in a more serious way. I signed up for adult education help and started blocking time instead of just saying I will get to it. I have also been baking more test batches because I am thinking about a home bakery. That means more careful grocery budgeting and more cleaning up flour than I expected.

follow_ups.question: What GED subject feels hardest?
follow_ups.response: Math, especially fractions and word problems. Reading and writing feel more natural.

follow_ups.question: Who tastes the bakery test batches?
follow_ups.response: Tommy, church friends, and Caleb, though Caleb will call anything good if it has sugar.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are grown now, so there is no school-year routine for them. When they were younger, mornings were packed lunches, bus timing, homework folders, and church youth group on Wednesdays. Marissa did choir and Caleb played a little football before deciding he liked fishing better. Now I help with Eli sometimes, and he is in preschool, so I hear about snack day and picture day again.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with Eli's weekday routine?
follow_ups.response: Only occasionally, if Marissa has an appointment or work conflict.

follow_ups.question: What kind of grandmother routine do you like best?
follow_ups.response: Saturday pancakes, reading him little books, and letting him water tomatoes with a small can.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Personally I have mostly had routine experiences, traffic stops, storm roadblocks, and officers helping with parade routes or football games. I have never been arrested. As a volunteer, I have dealt with police for permits and crowd control. Some officers are helpful and respectful; some talk down to people, and that bothers me.

follow_ups.question: When do you interact with police through volunteering?
follow_ups.response: Mostly for festivals, Mardi Gras routes, parking, and making sure food vendors are set where they are supposed to be.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever felt afraid during an interaction?
follow_ups.response: Not afraid for myself, but tense when an officer was sharp with young people hanging around after a game.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: After storms, seeing deputies direct traffic and check blocked roads stands out. Also, at football games they can either calm things down or make teenagers more wound up depending on their tone.

follow_ups.question: Do you know any officers personally?
follow_ups.response: A couple through church and events, not close friends.

follow_ups.question: Do people in your circle trust police?
follow_ups.response: It depends who you ask. Older white folks tend to trust more; some Black neighbors and younger people are more cautious.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have not been arrested. I had a cousin arrested years ago for DUI, and that shook the family because he could have hurt somebody.

follow_ups.question: Did that change how the family acted around drinking?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we got more serious about taking keys and having somebody drive.

follow_ups.question: Any recent arrests close to you?
follow_ups.response: No, not in my immediate family.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential elections and most local elections, though I have missed some smaller primaries. Local races matter to me because drainage, schools, police, and community centers touch daily life. I do not enjoy political arguing, but I do think voting is a responsibility. Tommy votes too, but he talks about it less.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide in local races?
follow_ups.response: I listen for who shows up, who knows the neighborhoods, and who talks plain about budgets.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever volunteer for campaigns?
follow_ups.response: No, I keep my volunteering nonpartisan through church and community events.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would say I am conservative-leaning, especially on faith, personal responsibility, and spending money carefully. I usually feel closer to Republicans, but I do not like mean politics or people acting like poor folks are lazy. I believe in helping neighbors, feeding children, and keeping seniors safe, and to me that is not a party thing. I want government to be careful with taxes, but I also know roads, schools, health clinics, and disaster response do not happen by magic. On social issues, I am traditional in my own life, but I try to treat people respectfully. My politics come from church, family, budgets, and living through storms more than from television.

follow_ups.question: What issues matter most to you?
follow_ups.response: Local jobs, disaster preparedness, schools, health care access, public safety, and not wasting taxpayer money.

follow_ups.question: Where do you get political information?
follow_ups.response: Local news, Facebook posts from officials, church conversations, and sometimes national news in the evening.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become less patient with party fighting. I used to vote more automatically Republican, and I still lean that way, but now I look harder at the person. After storms and health worries, I care more about competence than slogans. I also think more about how policies land on working families, because I see people at church stretched thin.

follow_ups.question: What made you less automatic about party?
follow_ups.response: Watching people argue on TV while local folks just needed help with roofs, medicine, and bills.

follow_ups.question: Have your church friends changed too?
follow_ups.response: Some have gotten more partisan. A few, like me, have gotten quieter and more practical.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It has affected me somewhat. I am a white woman in Mississippi, so I know I have not lived the same experiences as Black neighbors. Some of the national protests felt far away from my daily life, but the questions about fairness and policing are not far away. At church and events, I have seen how people can be treated differently or listened to differently.

follow_ups.question: Did any conversation change your thinking?
follow_ups.response: A Black woman I quilt with talked about worrying when her grandson drives at night, and that stayed with me.

follow_ups.question: Do you use the phrase Black Lives Matter yourself?
follow_ups.response: Not often, because it can start an argument fast here, but I understand why people are saying it.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think there are real issues around respect, fairness, and whether complaints get heard. I also think most local officers are not trying to do wrong, but systems and habits can still hurt people. My way of thinking is practical: train officers better, hold people accountable, and make sure young people are not treated like trouble before they do anything. I do not like when anyone turns it into hating all police or dismissing all racism.

follow_ups.question: Have you talked about this at church?
follow_ups.response: A little, mostly in careful side conversations, not from the pulpit.

follow_ups.question: What would accountability look like to you?
follow_ups.response: Body cameras used properly, supervisors taking complaints seriously, and officers who escalate too fast being corrected.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race is still part of everyday life, even when people wish it was not. In Mississippi, history is not old dust; it is in schools, neighborhoods, churches, and who had what opportunities. I try to listen more than speak when Black friends describe something I have not lived. I also think people need places to talk without being shamed right away, because shame makes folks shut down.

follow_ups.question: Does local history interest you in this way?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I read about Jackson County history, and you cannot separate local history from race, labor, churches, and land.

follow_ups.question: Do family members agree with you?
follow_ups.response: Some do. Some older relatives think talking about race just stirs trouble, and I disagree with that.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly talked with family and friends in small conversations. I have not joined protests, but I try not to shut down people who are hurting.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk with most openly?
follow_ups.response: Linda and one quilting friend named Patricia. They will speak honestly without turning it into a fight.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed anything you do?
follow_ups.response: I pay more attention to who gets heard in meetings and try to invite quieter people into decisions.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: It is mixed. Tommy thinks fairness matters but gets tired of national news yelling. Renee is more blunt and says people need to stop making excuses on all sides. Some church friends are sympathetic, and some think the whole movement is political. My younger relatives are more open to talking about racism than older ones.

follow_ups.question: Does this cause conflict in your family?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes at holidays if the TV is on. I usually change the subject before it ruins dinner.

follow_ups.question: Do your children see it differently?
follow_ups.response: Marissa is more sensitive to it, especially raising a child around diverse classmates. Caleb mostly avoids politics.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I am doing all right, but I have high blood pressure and my doctor has warned me about being prediabetic. I carry extra weight and have knee aches if I stand too long at events. I take a blood pressure pill, try to walk, and know I need to be more consistent with flossing and cutting back sweets. I can still do what I need to do, but I feel 49 in my knees some mornings.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see a doctor?
follow_ups.response: Usually twice a year unless something comes up.

follow_ups.question: What health habit are you most consistent with?
follow_ups.response: Taking my blood pressure medicine and walking when the weather allows.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easier when I have walking friends and fresh vegetables from the garden. It is harder because Southern food is comfort, baking is part of my life, and healthy groceries cost more. Heat also makes walking difficult in summer.

follow_ups.question: What healthy food do you actually enjoy?
follow_ups.response: Tomatoes, cucumbers, grilled fish, greens, and herbs like thyme in vegetables.

follow_ups.question: What food is hardest to limit?
follow_ups.response: Pecan pie and biscuits, especially when I am testing recipes.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: The main thing was being told my A1C was in the prediabetes range. That scared me because diabetes runs in my family. I also had a bad knee flare-up last fall after standing all weekend at a festival. No broken bones or hospital stays, but those two things made me take walking and weight more seriously.

follow_ups.question: What did the doctor recommend?
follow_ups.response: Lose some weight, walk regularly, reduce sweets and white bread, and come back for labs.

follow_ups.question: Did you follow through?
follow_ups.response: Partly. I walk more, but the baking makes the sugar part hard.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My knees slow me down at long events, so I plan chairs and breaks now. I can care for family, but I cannot pretend I can stand twelve hours like I did at 30.

follow_ups.question: Do you turn down volunteer work because of it?
follow_ups.response: Not usually, but I delegate more lifting and setup.

follow_ups.question: Does it affect housework?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I break mopping and deep cleaning into smaller pieces.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, my mama has arthritis and blood pressure issues, and she does not drive much anymore. I take her to appointments and help sort her medications. Tommy has had back strain from work, but he is stubborn about resting. Caregiving is not constant crisis, but it is a steady line running through the week.

follow_ups.question: How often do you help your mother?
follow_ups.response: Usually two or three times a week, plus phone calls.

follow_ups.question: Who helps you with caregiving?
follow_ups.response: My sister Renee splits some errands, though I do more scheduling.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have insurance through Tommy's work, but deductibles and copays still bite. I have put off dental cleanings and once delayed a follow-up because I was worried about the bill. Getting appointments can mean driving and waiting, and specialists are harder. We usually get necessary care, but we stretch timing and ask about payment.

follow_ups.question: What care gets delayed first?
follow_ups.response: Dental and eye appointments, because they feel less urgent until they are not.

follow_ups.question: Do you use urgent care?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, if it is after hours and not bad enough for the ER.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Mostly home remedies, not anything formal. We use honey and lemon for coughs, Epsom salt soaks, heating pads, herbal teas, and aloe from the yard for minor burns. I believe in doctors, but I also grew up with women knowing how to comfort ordinary aches at home. If it is serious, I call the clinic.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you those remedies?
follow_ups.response: My mama and grandmother, mostly by watching.

follow_ups.question: Do you use herbs from your garden this way?
follow_ups.response: Some lavender for calming scent and mint tea, but I am careful about not pretending herbs replace medicine.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I might have a small glass of wine at a wedding or holiday, but drinking is not my coping method. When I am stressed, I bake, clean, pray, walk, or call Linda. Sometimes I snack too much, which is its own problem.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever smoke?
follow_ups.response: No, I tried a cigarette as a teenager and hated it.

follow_ups.question: What do you do first when stress hits?
follow_ups.response: Usually make a list, because getting things out of my head calms me down.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I take my prescribed blood pressure medicine, and I use over-the-counter ibuprofen sometimes for my knee. I do not use marijuana or other drugs. The most recent was taking ibuprofen after a long choir and potluck day because my knee was throbbing. I try not to overdo it because I know medicine can cause problems too.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever use prescription pain medicine?
follow_ups.response: No, not currently.

follow_ups.question: Do people around you use marijuana?
follow_ups.response: I know some younger folks do, but it is not part of my life.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: We use Tommy's employer insurance and budget for copays. I keep a little medical envelope when I can, especially before lab work or dental visits. For Mama, Medicare helps, but prescriptions and rides still take planning. We compare prices on prescriptions and use generics whenever possible.

follow_ups.question: Do medical bills create debt for you?
follow_ups.response: Not big debt right now, but they can push other bills tight.

follow_ups.question: Who tracks appointments?
follow_ups.response: I do, in my paper planner and phone reminders.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally for vaccines, though I ask questions. I got COVID shots and flu shots because I am around older church members and my mama.

follow_ups.question: Were you nervous about the COVID vaccine?
follow_ups.response: A little at first, mostly because information was changing fast.

follow_ups.question: What helped you decide?
follow_ups.response: Talking to our clinic nurse and thinking about protecting Mama.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: I trust my doctor's office, our clinic nurse, the pharmacist, and the Mississippi Department of Health more than Facebook arguments. I may see something online, but I try to check it before repeating it. I also listen when people I know had side effects, but personal stories are not the same as medical advice.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss vaccine information at church?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially during COVID, but it could get tense.

follow_ups.question: Do you follow any health pages online?

follow_ups.question: Was it local to Moss Point?
follow_ups.response: Yes, local schools.

follow_ups.question: Did you visit her workplace?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, and I remember the smell of yeast rolls.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: Was he the main earner?
follow_ups.response: Yes, most of the time.

follow_ups.question: Did he work steady hours?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, with overtime when available.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Daddy worked in maintenance and repair around industrial and shipyard-related work. He fixed equipment, handled mechanical problems, and did practical hands-on work. He came home tired and smelling like metal, oil, and outside air.

follow_ups.question: Was he handy at home too?
follow_ups.response: Very. He fixed almost everything himself.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you practical skills?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially preparedness and not wasting supplies.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for industrial contractors connected to the coast's shipyard and plant economy. Those places repaired, maintained, and supported equipment and vessels. It was blue-collar Gulf Coast work.

follow_ups.question: Was the work dangerous?
follow_ups.response: It could be, so safety mattered.

follow_ups.question: Did his work shape your view of jobs?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I respect steady practical work and people who show up.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope I have my GED finished and maybe a certificate in early childhood education or health aide training. I would like a part-time paid role at the Moss Point Community Center or somewhere similar, coordinating volunteers and programs without giving up family time. I hope the bakery becomes a small legal home business, not huge, just enough to bring in income and make people happy. I want Tommy and me to have more savings, less credit card debt, and maybe take modest road trips to Gulf Shores, New Orleans, and Civil War history sites. I want my garden fuller, my knees stronger, my faith steady, and my family still coming to Sunday lunch.

follow_ups.question: What is the first step toward that future?
follow_ups.response: Passing the GED practice tests and scheduling the real exam sections.

follow_ups.question: What do you want to keep exactly the same?
follow_ups.response: Church, family meals, gardening, choir, and being someone people can count on.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value faith, family, usefulness, and keeping my word. I value hospitality, not fancy hospitality, but making sure people are fed, noticed, and not left alone. I value roots and local history because knowing where you come from helps you stand straighter. I also value practical kindness: the kind that brings a casserole, makes a phone call, balances the budget, and shows up after a storm.

follow_ups.question: What value do you hope your children see in you?
follow_ups.response: That love is action, not just talk.

follow_ups.question: What do you want people to count on you for?
follow_ups.response: Honesty, organization, food when needed, and a calm head in a mess.
